chapters.title: Chapter 1: Structure of U.S. Removal Adjudication and Appellate Review
chapters.description: Explains how immigration cases move from the immigration courts to the BIA and then to the courts of appeals, and how appellate courts review those decisions.
subtopics: Roles of DHS, Immigration Judges (IJs), and the Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA)
Single-member vs. panel BIA decisions
Petitions for review under 8 U.S.C. § 1252
Record rule: 8 U.S.C. § 1252(b)(4)(A)
Standards of review: substantial evidence for facts; de novo for legal issues
Consulting IJ reasoning when the BIA issues a brief affirmance
Relief-specific consolidation in final order review

chapters.title: Chapter 2: Asylum and Withholding of Removal—Core Framework
chapters.description: Sets out the statutory and regulatory foundations governing asylum and withholding, including who qualifies as a refugee and the protected grounds.
subtopics: INA definition of refugee: 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(42)(A)
Asylum eligibility and discretion: 8 U.S.C. § 1158
Protected grounds: race, religion, nationality, particular social group, political opinion
Withholding of removal: 8 U.S.C. § 1231(b)(3); 8 C.F.R. § 1208.16(b)
Standards of proof: well-founded fear vs. more-likely-than-not
Derivative status in asylum and non-derivative nature of withholding
Overview of CAT protection and its distinction from asylum/withholding

chapters.title: Chapter 3: Defining Past Persecution and the Cumulative Harm Approach
chapters.description: Details what constitutes persecution, emphasizing the cumulative assessment of harms and the line between serious persecution and lesser mistreatment.
subtopics: Persecution vs. harassment: severity, repetition, and context
Cumulative evaluation of multiple incidents
Physical harm, detention, property harm, coercion
Psychological and emotional harm: evidentiary considerations
Threats-only claims and when threats may suffice
Private-actor persecution: threshold showing

chapters.title: Chapter 4: Nexus to a Protected Ground and Mixed-Motive Analysis
chapters.description: Explains the requirement that persecution be on account of a protected ground and how courts assess motive, including mixed motives.
subtopics: The ‘one central reason’ standard: 8 U.S.C. § 1158(b)(1)(B)(i)
Evidence of motive: direct statements, timing, circumstantial indicators
Imputed political opinion
Distinguishing personal disputes, criminal motives, and extortion from protected-ground persecution
Mixed motives: when a protected ground is central vs. incidental or tangential
Burden of proof on nexus

chapters.title: Chapter 5: Government Unable or Unwilling to Protect
chapters.description: Covers the requirement to show that the government either perpetrated the harm or was unable or unwilling to control private persecutors.
subtopics: Doctrinal test for state protection
Notice and reporting to authorities: significance and proof
Futility and danger exceptions to reporting
Assessing governmental efforts: investigations, arrests, protective measures
Systemic vs. isolated failures of protection
Country-conditions evidence and institutional capacity

chapters.title: Chapter 6: Well-Founded Fear of Future Persecution
chapters.description: Explores how applicants prove a forward-looking fear of persecution, with and without a past-persecution presumption.
subtopics: Subjective and objective components
Presumption from past persecution and rebuttal
Pattern-or-practice claims
Individualized risk vs. generalized violence
Evidentiary sources: testimony, corroboration, country reports

chapters.title: Chapter 7: Internal Relocation and Changed Circumstances
chapters.description: Explains when internal relocation defeats a fear of future persecution and how reasonableness is evaluated.
subtopics: Regulatory framework: 8 C.F.R. § 1208.13(b)(1)–(3) (asylum) and § 1208.16(b) (withholding)
Burden allocation depending on past persecution and persecutor type
Reasonableness factors: safety, economic practicality, social ties, and access to services
Persecutor’s reach and the role of family safety
Fundamental change in circumstances vs. relocation

chapters.title: Chapter 8: Particular Social Group (PSG) Doctrine
chapters.description: Provides the foundational criteria and pitfalls in defining PSGs and connecting them to the harm.
subtopics: Immutable characteristics, particularity, and social distinction
Circularity and overbreadth problems
PSG vs. nexus: separate inquiries
Common PSG archetypes and evidentiary showings
Country-specific social distinction evidence
Interaction with mixed-motive analysis

chapters.title: Chapter 9: Withholding of Removal—Higher Standard and Key Distinctions
chapters.description: Focuses on the mandatory nature, burdens, and differences from asylum that often determine case outcomes.
subtopics: ‘Clear probability’/more-likely-than-not standard
No discretionary denial; no derivative beneficiaries
No one-year filing bar; different nexus standard equivalency
Interplay with internal relocation and state protection
Remedy scope and practical consequences

chapters.title: Chapter 10: Evidentiary Rules, Credibility, and Corroboration in Asylum Cases
chapters.description: Covers how testimony is assessed, the role of corroboration, and the impact of credibility on burdens of proof.
subtopics: REAL ID Act standards: 8 U.S.C. § 1158(b)(1)(B)(ii)–(iii)
Credibility factors and inconsistencies
When corroboration is required and how to obtain it
Country-conditions reports and expert testimony
Weight of affidavits and secondary evidence
Adverse credibility vs. credible but insufficient claims

chapters.title: Chapter 11: Issue Preservation, Exhaustion, Waiver, and Abandonment
chapters.description: Explains the procedural prerequisites to appellate review and how failure to raise issues can forfeit them.
subtopics: Statutory exhaustion: 8 U.S.C. § 1252(d)(1)
Raising issues before the IJ and BIA
Waiver and abandonment on appeal
Chenery and limits on post hoc rationales
Consequences for CAT and due process claims not pursued

chapters.title: Chapter 12: Due Process and the Right to Counsel in Removal Proceedings
chapters.description: Outlines procedural protections afforded in immigration court, including representation rights and the prejudice standard.
subtopics: Right to counsel at no government expense
Notice, opportunity to be heard, and impartial adjudicator
Interpreter and evidentiary fairness
Prejudice requirement for due process violations
Continuances to obtain counsel and related standards

chapters.title: Chapter 13: Distinguishing Political Persecution from Criminal Targeting
chapters.description: Provides tools for differentiating protected-ground motives from criminal or personal motives often present in extortion or gang/narco contexts.
subtopics: Economic motives vs. political motives
Personal vendettas and property disputes
Evidence that converts criminal conduct into political persecution
Imputed political opinion and anti-corruption claims
Assessing statements by perpetrators and temporal links

chapters.title: Landmark Foundations I: Niang v. Gonzales and the Asylum Elements
chapters.description: Covers Niang’s articulation of the statutory refugee definition and the three elements of past persecution, including the state-protection prong.
subtopics: Refugee definition and core asylum elements
Past persecution as a gateway to future-fear presumption
Government ‘unable or unwilling’ component within the elements
Effect on burden shifting for future fear

chapters.title: Landmark Foundations II: Rivera-Barrientos and Dallakoti on Nexus and ‘One Central Reason’
chapters.description: Explains the Tenth Circuit’s leading nexus doctrine, emphasizing when a protected ground is central rather than incidental in mixed-motive cases.
subtopics: Statutory ‘one central reason’ standard
Mixed-motive analysis and evidentiary showings
‘Incidental, tangential, superficial, or subordinate’ motives
Application to political-opinion and PSG claims

chapters.title: Landmark Foundations III: Wiransane and Karki on the Persecution Threshold and Threats
chapters.description: Summarizes Tenth Circuit guidance on what rises to persecution and why threats alone generally do not suffice, while physical injury is not strictly required.
subtopics: Persecution defined beyond ‘restrictions or threats’
Cumulative-harm lens for multiple incidents
Threats-only doctrine and exceptions
Role of psychological harm without physical injury

chapters.title: Landmark Foundations IV: Singh v. Bondi on State Protection, Reporting, and Futility
chapters.description: Highlights recent Tenth Circuit guidance on the ‘unable or unwilling’ prong, focusing on reporting, governmental notice, and the futility-or-danger exception.
subtopics: Importance of reporting past harm to authorities
Assessing government response and protective efforts
When failure to report is excused
Implications for private-actor persecution claims
